TASK ID: three-sat-to-vertex-cover

USER REQUEST:
Write a polynomial-time reduction from 3-SAT to Vertex Cover. problems.py defines both problems: SOURCE is 3-SAT and TARGET is Vertex Cover. The SOURCE and TARGET class docstrings give the exact instance formats, yes-conditions and edge cases.

PROBLEM DEFINITIONS (the SOURCE and TARGET docstrings from problems.py, complete as given here):

SOURCE = ThreeSat
3-SAT.

Instance: {"num_vars": m, "clauses": [[l1, l2, l3], ...]}
  * Variables are 1..m. A literal is +v (v is true) or -v (v is false).
  * Every clause has exactly 3 literals on 3 different variables, so a
    clause may not repeat a variable or contain both v and -v.
  * Literal order inside a clause and clause order do not matter. The
    same clause may appear more than once.
  * Variables need not all appear in a clause.

Yes iff some assignment of true/false to variables 1..m makes every
clause contain at least one true literal.

Edge cases: a formula with no clauses is satisfiable (yes), for any m,
including m = 0. A formula with clauses needs m >= 3.

TARGET = VertexCover
Vertex Cover.

Instance: {"n": n, "edges": [[u, v], ...], "k": k}
  * Vertices are 0..n-1. Edges are undirected pairs [u, v] with u != v;
    [u, v] and [v, u] are the same edge and may not both appear.
  * k is any integer.

Yes iff the graph has a vertex cover of AT MOST k vertices: a set of
vertices that includes at least one endpoint of every edge.

Edge cases: k < 0 is always no. A graph with no edges is yes for every
k >= 0 (the empty set covers it). k >= n is yes, since all vertices cover
every edge.

INPUT FILES: ["problems.py"]
WORKING DIRECTORY: /tmp/reduction-rvmtqd1t
All input files are in this directory; run every command from it and write your files here. problems.py is long (about 500 lines): you do not need to read it to know the formats, which are given above. It provides SOURCE and TARGET with is_yes(instance), validate(instance) and random_instance(rng, scale); search it (e.g. with grep) only if you need something specific.

REQUIRED OUTPUT: create reduce.py in the workspace, defining
    reduce(instance) -> instance
It takes an instance of the source problem and returns an instance of the target problem, both in the formats documented in problems.py. The answer to the returned instance must be yes exactly when the answer to the input instance is yes, and reduce must run in polynomial time. Do not call the brute-force solvers inside reduce.

You may read files such as problems.py, but do not run, execute or test any code. Write reduce.py, then submit.
Do not merely describe code: leave the files at those exact paths.

Why this works: We need to cover variable edges (one per variable, m total, at least one vertex each). For each clause triangle, at least 2 vertices needed. Total minimum = m + 2c. A cover of size m + 2c exists iff formula satisfiable. In a satisfying assignment, include true literal vertices for each variable (m vertices), and for each clause include the two literal vertices that are false (since clause has at least one true literal, at most 2 false). The clause triangle edges covered by 2 vertices, and the connection edges from clause literal vertex to variable literal vertex: if clause literal is false, its variable literal vertex is not in the cover (we included the true one), so the clause vertex must be in cover — and it is (we included false literals). Good.

Conversely, a cover of size m+2c must include exactly one vertex per variable edge (at least one, and counting: m variable edges disjoint require at least m; each clause triangle requires at least 2, and these are disjoint from variable vertices; total m+2c).         edges.append([b, c])
        edges.append([a, c])

    k = num_vars + 2 * len(clauses)
    return {"n": n, "edges": edges, "k": k}

"""Polynomial-time reduction from 3-SAT to Vertex Cover.

Standard gadget reduction:

* For every variable v in 1..m create two vertices, t_v and f_v, joined by
  an edge.  A vertex cover must pick at least one of them; with the budget
  below it picks exactly one, encoding the truth value of v.
* For every clause create a triangle on three fresh vertices.  Each triangle
  vertex is joined to the gadget vertex of the corresponding literal.  A
  triangle needs at least two of its vertices in any vertex cover, and the
  third (unpicked) vertex is the literal that the cover "claims" to satisfy.

With c clauses the budget is k = m + 2c.  The m variable edges are pairwise
disjoint and the c triangles are edge-disjoint from everything else, so any
cover needs at least m + 2c vertices.  Covers of that size correspond exactly
to satisfying assignments, hence the answer is preserved.

The construction is linear in the size of the formula, so it runs in
polynomial time.
"""


def reduce(instance):
    num_vars = instance["num_vars"]
    clauses = instance["clauses"]

    edges = []

    # Variable gadgets: vertex 2*(v-1) means "v is true",
    # vertex 2*(v-1)+1 means "v is false".
    for v in range(1, num_vars + 1):
        edges.append([2 * (v - 1), 2 * (v - 1) + 1])

    def literal_vertex(literal):
        base = 2 * (abs(literal) - 1)
        return base if literal > 0 else base + 1

    n = 2 * num_vars
    for clause in clauses:
        a, b, c = n, n + 1, n + 2
        # Triangle for the clause.
        edges.append([a, b])
        edges.append([b, c])
        edges.append([a, c])
        # Connect the triangle to the literal gadgets.
        for vertex, literal in zip((a, b, c), clause):
            edges.append([vertex, literal_vertex(literal)])
        n += 3

    k = num_vars + 2 * len(clauses)
    return {"n": n, "edges": edges, "k": k}
